1268.title: Led around the fire
1268.hook: a couple ties a knot and walks around a fire. the Rig Veda's wedding hymn says why: the bride is led around Agni first
1268.carry: agni, the fire, is witness to the wedding vow
1268.tomorrow: The hymn that quotes its doubters
1268.howItsDone: At many Hindu weddings the couple walks around a sacred fire while verses are chanted, some of them from the Rig Veda's wedding hymn (10.85), with Agni treated as witness to the vows.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Krishna in the Gita: among meters, I am the Gayatri. Vibhuti: God shows through the best of each thing.

A wedding hall. A small fire in a square of bricks, a priest chanting, and a couple, tied together by a knotted scarf, walking slowly around the flame while the family throws rice and petals. Somebody's little cousin asks the obvious question: why are they walking around a fire? The answer goes back to a wedding in the Rig Veda, and the bride is the daughter of the Sun. This week, four of the Veda's voices. Today: Agni, the fire, at a wedding.
screen: `A KNOTTED SCARF. A SMALL FLAME.` → `WHY WALK AROUND A FIRE?` → `A WEDDING IN THE RIG VEDA.`

segments.voice: The Rig Veda's wedding hymn, book ten, hymn eighty-five, tells of the marriage of Surya, the daughter of the Sun. In paraphrase: her mind was her wagon, the sky its canopy, and two bright oxen drew it. Soma, the moon, was the groom, and the Ashvins, the twin horsemen gods, rode along as the wedding escort. A wedding with the whole sky invited. Then the hymn comes down to the ground, to a human wedding, and the god it turns to is Agni. In paraphrase: to you, Agni, they first led Surya around, with her bridal train. Give the wife to her husband, Agni, with children to come. The bride is led around the fire first. Agni receives her and gives her into her new life. Another verse is the groom's: I take your hand for good fortune. Verses from this hymn are still recited at many Hindu weddings. Here's the teaching. In the Vedas, Agni is the go-between: what is placed in the fire reaches the gods. So a promise made beside the fire isn't made only to a spouse. It's made in front of the gods, with Agni as witness. That's why Hindus marry before a sacred fire and walk around it, the rounds many families call the pheras. People call such a marriage agni sakshi: with fire as witness. The flame isn't decoration. It's the guest who carries the vow up.

segments.voice: If you can, light a diya or a candle, safely, and sit where you can see it; if not, picture a wedding fire you've seen. Bring to mind one promise you've made, to a person, to God, or to yourself. Say it quietly in front of the flame, as if Agni were listening and carrying it up. If you pray, ask for help keeping it. If you don't, let the flame simply be your witness.
Hymns to Agni. Today, Agni at the wedding: the fire the bride is led around first, witness to the vow. Today's word.
Your line: agni, the fire, is witness to the wedding vow. The promise goes up with the flame. See you tomorrow.

1269.title: The hymn that quotes its doubters
1269.hook: "where is he?" some ask. "he is not," some say. a hymn to Indra quotes its doubters out loud
1269.carry: shraddha: trust you place, even beside doubt
1269.howItsDone: Hymns to Indra are part of the Rig Veda's recitation, kept in Vedic schools; in later Hindu stories Indra appears as king of the gods and lord of rain.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Agni the fire, at the wedding: witness to the vow.

"Where is he?" people ask. "He isn't real," others answer. It could be an argument at a dinner table this week. It's a line from a hymn in the Rig Veda, book two, and the god being doubted is Indra: the storm, the warrior, the one who breaks the dam and lets the rivers run. The hymn could have left the doubters out. Instead it quotes them, right in the middle of the praise. Today: the second voice, Indra.
screen: `"WHERE IS HE?"` → `"HE ISN'T REAL."` → `A HYMN THAT QUOTES ITS DOUBTERS.`

segments.voice: Indra is the mighty one of the Rig Veda's storms. In its stories he fights Vritra, a serpent coiled around the waters, and when Indra strikes him down, the rivers pour free. Book two, hymn twelve, praises him in a shape you can hear even in paraphrase. Verse after verse tells something he did: he steadied the shaking earth, spread out the sky, killed the serpent and set the rivers flowing. And verse after verse ends the same way. Sa janasa indrah. He, O people, is Indra. Then, in the fifth verse, the hymn turns. In paraphrase: the terrible one, about whom they ask, where is he? About whom they say, he is not. The singer's answer isn't an argument. It's shrad asmai dhatta: put your trust in him. Listen to those two phrases, because Hindu tradition still uses them. He is not has na asti in it: is not. The same two words later give Sanskrit its word nastika, one who says, there is not. And put your trust holds the roots of shraddha: faith, trust you choose to place, which many scholars hear as setting your heart on something. Here's the teaching. The Veda doesn't hide doubt. It names the doubter in his own words, and answers with shraddha, not proof. Centuries later the Gita says a person is made of their shraddha: as your trust is, so are you.
screen: `"HE, O PEOPLE, IS INDRA."` · `"WHERE IS HE?" "HE IS NOT."` · `NA ASTI → NASTIKA.` · `SHRAD DHATTA → SHRADDHA: TRUST YOU PLACE.`

segments.voice: Let one honest doubt be asked, about God, or whether any of this is true, without arguing it away. Then do what the hymn does: place your trust somewhere, even something small: a name of God you grew up with, the people who taught you, the breath coming back. If you pray, say that name once, slowly, and let the doubt sit beside it. If you don't, simply notice where your trust already rests.
Hymns to Agni, and today, to Indra. In Rig Veda two, twelve, each verse ends, he, O people, is Indra; one verse quotes those who say, he is not, and answers, put your trust in him. Today's word.
Your line: shraddha, trust you place, even beside doubt. The hymn kept the doubter's words and still sang. Go gently.

1270.title: One dawn, different lives
1270.hook: a wedding house at dawn: one cooks, one calls, one prays. the Rig Veda's dawn wakes each creature to its own way of living
1270.carry: svadharma: the dawn wakes each to their own path
1270.tomorrow: The boy bound to the post
1270.howItsDone: Many Hindus keep the hours around sunrise for prayer, bathing and the morning sandhya; in many homes the day starts with a verse said while looking at the palms, karagre vasate lakshmih, whose wording varies by family.

screen: `"HE IS NOT." AND THE ANSWER: SHRADDHA.`

segments.voice: Five-thirty in the morning on a wedding day. One aunt is already frying puris. An uncle is on the phone about the flowers. A cousin is asleep with her mehndi drying, and a grandmother stands at the window, palms together. Same house, same gray light coming in, and everyone wakes to a different job. A Rig Veda poet watched the dawn do exactly that to a whole world. Today: the third voice, Ushas, the dawn.
screen: `ONE HOUSE, FIVE-THIRTY A.M.` → `EVERYONE WAKES TO A DIFFERENT JOB.` → `USHAS, THE DAWN.`

segments.voice: In the Rig Veda, Ushas is the dawn and a goddess, a young woman in bright clothes who opens the doors of the dark. Book one, hymn one hundred thirteen, watches what she does when she comes. In paraphrase: one she wakes to power, one to fame, one to greatness, one to go after his own aim. To see their different ways of living, the dawn has woken every creature. That's the picture: one light, and under it a hundred lives starting up, none of them the same, all woken by the same goddess. The hymn doesn't rank them. It watches each one go. Hindu tradition has a big word for that idea: svadharma, your own dharma, the path that is yours to walk. Centuries later, in the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna tells Arjuna: better your own dharma, done imperfectly, than another's done well. In the Gita it first means Arjuna's duty as a warrior; many teachers today read it as each person's own path. Either way, it starts in the morning. That's why so many Hindu homes treat waking as a small rite. In one common morning verse, you look at your palms before anything else: at the fingertips lives Lakshmi, in the middle Sarasvati, at the root Govinda. Your own two hands, the first thing you see, the place your own day's work begins.
screen: `USHAS OPENS THE DOORS OF THE DARK.` · `ONE LIGHT, A HUNDRED LIVES.` · `SVADHARMA: YOUR OWN PATH.` · `LOOK AT YOUR PALMS FIRST.`

segments.voice: Open your hands and look at your palms, the way the morning verse asks. If you pray, say it, or its meaning: Lakshmi at the fingertips, Sarasvati in the middle, Govinda at the root. If you don't, just look at your hands and ask: what's mine to do today? Name one thing that belongs to your path, not anyone else's, and let it be enough for this morning.
Hymns to Agni, and today, to Ushas: the dawn who wakes every creature to its own way of living. Today's word.
Your line: svadharma, the dawn wakes each to their own path. Look at your hands first. Until tomorrow.

1271.title: The boy bound to the post
1271.hook: a king promises a god his son, then stalls for years. Varuna, keeper of vows, comes to collect
1271.carry: varuna keeps the vow, and loosens the bond
1271.howItsDone: Many Hindus keep a vrata, a vow such as a weekly fast, a temple visit or a pilgrimage promised to God, and treat finishing it as serious; Rig Veda 1.24, credited to Shunahshepa, is part of Vedic recitation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ushas, the dawn. Svadharma: the dawn wakes each to their own path.

A king with everything except a child makes a deal with a god: give me a son, and I'll give him back to you. The son is born. The god comes to collect. And the king says, not yet, he's only a baby. Then, not yet, wait until his teeth come in. Then, wait until they fall out. Anyone who has ever said we'll talk about it later knows the move. The god is Varuna. Today: the fourth voice, and a promise that comes due.
screen: `GIVE ME A SON.` → `NOT YET. NOT YET. NOT YET.` → `THE GOD IS VARUNA.`

segments.voice: The story is told in the Aitareya Brahmana, a prose text of the Rig Veda. King Harishchandra prays to Varuna, the god who keeps rita, the order of truth, and vows: if a son is born, I'll offer him to you. Rohita is born, and the king stalls until the boy is grown. Then Rohita takes his bow and runs to the forest, and Varuna seizes the king with a swelling sickness. Years later Rohita meets a starving sage, Ajigarta, and buys his middle son, Shunahshepa, for a hundred cows, to go in his place. The boy is bound to the post. His own father comes forward with a knife. And Shunahshepa does the one thing left. He prays. In the telling he goes from god to god, Prajapati, Agni, Savitr, Varuna, Indra, the Ashvins, and at last Ushas, the dawn, and with each verse to the dawn a cord falls away. With the last, he is free, and the king is well. The sage Vishvamitra takes the boy as his own son. Hymns in the Rig Veda are credited to Shunahshepa, and one asks: loosen, Varuna, the upper bond, the middle, and the lowest. Here's the teaching. In the hymns Varuna is dhritavrata, the one who holds to vows, and vrata is the word Hindus still use for a vow kept to God, a fast, a pilgrimage, a promise. A vow is a bond, and Varuna holds people to theirs. But the same god who binds is the one who unties.
screen: `A VOW TO VARUNA, STALLED.` · `SHUNAHSHEPA, BOUND TO THE POST.` · `EACH VERSE TO DAWN, A CORD FALLS.` · `VRATA: A VOW IS A BOND.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one promise you keep putting off: to a person, to God, or to yourself. Don't scold yourself. Just say it plainly, the way Harishchandra never did: this is what I said I'd do. If you pray, borrow Shunahshepa's words: loosen what binds me, the upper, the middle, the lowest. If you don't, choose one small step toward keeping it today.
Hymns to Agni, and today, to Varuna: keeper of rita and of vows, who holds a stalling king to his word and unties a boy who prays. Today's word.
Your line: varuna keeps the vow, and loosens the bond. A promise to God is worth keeping. That's today, done.

1272.title: The twin healers
1272.hook: a woman loses a leg in battle; a man is left at sea. the same twin gods arrive both times: the Ashvins
1272.carry: the ashvins: healing is holy work
1272.howItsDone: Ayurveda's classic texts trace medical knowledge from the gods through the Ashvins to human sages; many Hindu families pray for the sick alongside medical care, and some honor Dhanvantari, the god of Ayurveda, on Dhanteras.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a king who stalled his vow, and a boy set free. Varuna keeps the vow, and loosens the bond.
screen: `VARUNA KEEPS THE VOW, AND LOOSENS THE BOND.`

segments.voice: A woman goes into battle at night and loses a leg, cut off, the hymn says, like the wing of a bird. A young man is left behind in the sea, three days and nights, with nothing to hold on to. In both stories the same two arrive, fast, in a chariot: twin gods, always called together, never one without the other. They give the woman a leg of iron to walk on. They carry the man home. Today: the gods who come as a pair, the Ashvins.
screen: `A LEG LOST IN BATTLE.` → `A MAN LEFT AT SEA.` → `THE SAME TWO ARRIVE.`

segments.voice: The Ashvins are the twin horsemen of the Rig Veda. Sanskrit even names them in a form kept just for two: Ashvinau, the pair. They're called at daybreak, alongside Ushas, and a long hymn, book one, hymn one hundred sixteen, is a list of their rescues. Bhujyu, left in the sea, carried home in ships that moved by themselves. Vishpala, whose leg was cut off in a night battle: the twins gave her a leg of iron, so she could walk when the fighting was done. A blind man given back his sight. The old sage Chyavana, made young again. Over and over, someone is in trouble, and the twins come. Later tradition calls them the physicians of the gods. The Charaka Samhita, a great classic of Ayurveda, traces its own knowledge down a line that runs from Brahma, through the Ashvins, to Indra, and from Indra to human sages. Here's the teaching. In Hindu tradition, healing isn't outside religion. The gods have their own doctors, and medicine is pictured as knowledge handed down from them. So a family can do puja in the morning and see the surgeon in the afternoon, and neither cancels the other. You could say that for the Vedic poets, a healer arriving in time looked like the gods themselves showing up.

1273.title: The prayer at the river
1273.hook: ten kings against one, at a river. the Rig Veda remembers the battle by a family's prayer, and how they always end it

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Ashvins in the Rig Veda, the twin healers. The Ashvins: healing is holy work.

Ten kings, joined against one. In the Rig Veda's seventh book, King Sudas faces an alliance of ten, near a river called the Parushni. His priest is the sage Vasishtha. The odds are terrible. And what the hymns remember isn't a battle plan. It's a prayer. Vasishtha's family called on Indra, the hymns say, and Indra heard them. Today, the last day on these four voices: what Vasishtha's family asks for at the end, every time.
screen: `TEN KINGS AGAINST ONE.` → `NOT A BATTLE PLAN. A PRAYER.` → `HOW THE HYMNS END.`

segments.voice: The battle of the ten kings is one of the few events in the Rig Veda that reads like history, and it's remembered in the hymns of Vasishtha's family. In paraphrase, from book seven: like thirsting men, surrounded in the battle of the ten kings, they looked up to the sky, and Indra heard Vasishtha as he praised him. Another hymn gives the victory to Indra and Varuna together: the ten kings could not overcome Sudas. Now listen to how so many of this family's hymns end. Not with a boast. With one line, the same line, hymn after hymn: yuyam pata svastibhih sada nah. You all, protect us always with blessings. Yuyam is you, plural: all of you, every god at once. Svasti is well-being, things going well. After praise of Indra, after a plea to Varuna, after a song to the dawn, the sign-off doesn't change. Here's the teaching. Asking the gods for svasti, well-being, is one of the oldest prayers Hindus have, and it's still said. Another Rig Veda verse, chanted today as a peace prayer before study and worship, is a string of them: svasti na indro, may Indra give us well-being; may Pushan, may the great bird Tarkshya, may Brihaspati. When you don't know which god to ask, the hymns' answer is simple: ask them all, and ask for well-being.
screen: `TEN KINGS. INDRA HEARD VASISHTHA.` · `YUYAM PATA SVASTIBHIH SADA NAH.` · `YUYAM: ALL OF YOU.` · `SVASTI NA INDRO: STILL CHANTED.`

End the way the hymns end, the same way every time: keep us well, always.

A king holds a great sacrifice, and his singers take their places. Into the hall walks a ragged man. Not long before, in a famine, he was eating a stranger's leftover beans. Now he sits down beside the king's chanters, and as they begin, he turns to each one: if you sing this without knowing the god it belongs to, your head will fall off. The singing stops. His name is Ushasti, and the songs are the Sama Veda's. Today: the Veda as song.
screen: `A RAGGED MAN AT THE KING'S RITE.` → `"DO YOU KNOW WHAT YOU'RE SINGING TO?"` → `THE VEDA AS SONG.`

segments.voice: The Sama Veda is the Veda of melodies. Saman means a chant, and its verses are ones that also appear in the Rig Veda, gathered and set to tune for the singers of the rite. It even opens with a call to the fire: agna a yahi vitaye, come, Agni, to the feast. In the great rites some priests recited and others sang, led by the udgatri, the chief singer. Those are the singers Ushasti stops, in the Chandogya Upanishad, a text of the Sama Veda. The king, alarmed, asks who he is, and hires him on the spot. Then the singers ask: so what are the gods of our chants? He tells them. The opening chant belongs to breath, because every creature enters and leaves life with breath. The high chant belongs to the sun, because every creature sings to it when it rises high. The response belongs to food, because every creature lives by taking it in. Breath, sun, food: what keeps you alive is what you're singing to. Near its start the same Upanishad puts the teaching in one line: what is done with knowledge, with faith, and with its inner meaning becomes stronger. That's why Hindu tradition prizes melody and meaning together. The tune carries the words in; knowing what they mean lets you sing them on purpose. A bhajan, an aarti, a mantra at a havan: sung knowing what it says, it is more than sound.
screen: `SAMAN: A CHANT, A MELODY.` · `"DO YOU KNOW THE GOD OF YOUR CHANT?"` · `BREATH. THE SUN. FOOD.` · `KNOWLEDGE AND FAITH MAKE IT STRONGER.`

segments.voice: Choose one line you know by heart: an aarti, a bhajan, a mantra, or simply Om. Before you sing it, think for a moment about what it means; if you aren't sure, hold the one word you do know. Then sing or hum it once, slowly, meaning it; if you can't make sound where you are, say it silently. If you don't pray, use a line from a song that matters to you.
